context_blurb:
Stars are born, shine and die, and one thing decides how: a star's mass, the amount of matter it holds. A star like the Sun shines for billions of years and ends as a small, fading ember; a giant blazes briefly, then explodes.

Stars are born in nebulae, huge clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls each clump inward while the heat in its gas pushes outward, and warmer gas pushes harder. Only in the coldest, densest clumps does cold gas push back too weakly to resist gravity, so the clump collapses into a protostar, a young star that heats up as it shrinks.

A star of 16 Suns has 16 times the Sun's fuel, yet lasts some 10 million years to the Sun's 10 billion. Holding up its weight takes more pressure in its core, so the core is hotter, and a hotter core burns its fuel far faster, thousands of times faster than the Sun's.

Colour shows a star's surface temperature: the hotter the surface, the bluer the light. In Orion, blue-white Rigel's surface is about 11,800 degrees Celsius and orange-red Betelgeuse's about 3,300. So Rigel's surface is far hotter than Betelgeuse's. Many people, thinking of fire, take red for hottest; it means cooler.

Ejnar Hertzsprung in 1911 and Henry Norris Russell in 1913 each charted stars by surface temperature and luminosity, the light a star truly gives off. Nine stars in ten, the Sun included, fall in one band of this Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, the main sequence. When the Sun's core fuel runs low, its outer layers will balloon and cool, so it will glow red yet shine far more, being so vast: brighter, with a cooler surface, a red giant.

A red giant then puffs its outer layers into space. William Herschel named such glowing shells planetary nebulae because they looked like planets' discs, but they have nothing to do with planets. The Ring Nebula is one: gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star around its hot leftover core, a white dwarf. The Sun will end this way.

Sirius B, the white dwarf beside bright Sirius, has a surface over four times the Sun's temperature yet gives under a tenth of the Sun's light, for light depends on both heat and size. Sirius B packs about the Sun's mass into a ball about the size of Earth: white-hot all over, but tiny.

Electrons hold a white dwarf up: squeezed close, they resist being packed tighter. In 1930 the 19-year-old Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar asked how heavy a white dwarf could be, using Einstein's special relativity: in a heavier one the electrons near the speed of light, and their push falls behind gravity. The older sums, without relativity, set no ceiling. His own first figure was about 0.91 Suns, for stars' make-up was then misjudged; today's sums give at most about 1.4 times the Sun's mass. Above that, a dead core collapses into a neutron star or a black hole.

When Chandrasekhar presented his limit in London in 1935, Arthur Eddington, Britain's leading astrophysicist, attacked it at once. Eddington, who had shown how a star's brightness follows from its mass, accepted white dwarfs, but a dead star collapsing with nothing to halt it struck him as absurd: Nature, he declared, should have a law against it. Niels Bohr and Wolfgang Pauli agreed with Chandrasekhar but stayed out of the public quarrel; Eddington never recanted. The evidence sided with the younger man: weighed white dwarfs fall below the limit, and in 1983 Chandrasekhar shared the Nobel Prize in Physics.

Stars above about eight Suns swell into brilliant supergiants, and when the spent core can no longer bear its weight, it collapses and the star explodes as a supernova. The guest star that Song dynasty astronomers logged in 1054 was a massive star exploding as a supernova. Its wreckage is the Crab Nebula, still rushing outward.

At its heart spins the core the blast left, a neutron star heavier than the Sun yet about 20 kilometres across. In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a graduate student, spotted what she called a bit of scruff on a new radio telescope's charts: pulses every 1.337 seconds, steady as a clock. The source was a neutron star spinning very fast, sweeping a radio beam past Earth like a lighthouse: a pulsar. In 1968 the Crab's own pulsar, flashing about 30 times a second, proved too fast for anything else. Her supervisor, Antony Hewish, shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics; Bell was left out.
